nodes.name: Ni3Sn2 synthesis
nodes.procedure: PEG 4000 (1000 mg), NiCl2·6H2O (356 mg), and SnCl2·2H2O (225 mg) were dispersed in 55 mL of ethylene glycol. The mixture was placed in a three-necked Schlenk flask equipped with a reflux condenser under nitrogen protection and heated to 150°C. After complete dissolution of all the solids, the temperature was gradually increased to 170°C, and the liquid mixture started to reflux. A suspension of NaBH4 (350 mg) in ethanol (10 mL) was then slowly added dropwise over 20 min. One neck of the flask was kept open to release the excess pressure caused by ethanol evaporation. The reaction was maintained under reflux for an additional 30 min and then cooled to room temperature. The resulting solid was washed thoroughly with deionized water and ethanol, followed by vacuum drying at 60°C for 12 h to obtain Ni3Sn2.

nodes.name: Carbon support loading
nodes.procedure: The prepared samples (40 mg) and Vulcan XC-72R carbon black (60 mg) were separately dispersed in cyclohexane solution (150 mL). The suspension with the sample was gradually added dropwise into the suspension with carbon under ultrasonication. The mixture was stirred at 30°C for 48 h. The product was then collected, washed with ethanol, vacuum-dried at 60°C for 12 h, and finally calcined under an Ar atmosphere at 250°C for 2 h to obtain the final catalyst.

nodes.name: NiOOH-SnO₃²⁻ electrochemical reconstruction
nodes.procedure: NiOOH-SnO₃²⁻ electrodes were prepared through electrochemical activation of Ni₃Sn₂/C catalyst. Cyclic voltammetry was conducted from 1.0 to 1.5 V_RHE for 100 cycles in 1.0 M KOH solution containing 0.5 M urea at a scan rate of 50 mV s⁻¹.
nodes.source_text: Synthesis of NiOOH-SnO₃ and NiOOH: NiOOH-SnO₃ and NiOOH electrodes were prepared through electrochemical activation of Ni₃Sn₂ and Ni NPs, respectively. Cyclic voltammetry was conducted from 1.0 to 1.5 V_RHE for 100 cycles in 1.0 M KOH solution containing 0.5 M urea at a scan rate of 50 mVs⁻¹.

nodes.name: NiOOH synthesis
nodes.procedure: A control sample of Ni nanoparticles (Ni NPs) was synthesized using the same method without the addition of SnCl2·2H2O. NiOOH electrodes were prepared through electrochemical activation of Ni NPs. Cyclic voltammetry was conducted from 1.0 to 1.5 VRHE for 100 cycles in 1.0 M KOH solution containing 0.5 M urea at a scan rate of 50 mV s^-1.

nodes.characterization_summary: Powder XRD pattern of Ni₃Sn₂ matches well with hexagonal Ni₃Sn₂ (PDF# 44-1418, space group P63/mcm).
nodes.evidence_snippet: The powder X-ray diffraction (XRD) pattern (Figure 1b) of the sample matches well with hexagonal Ni₃Sn₂ (PDF# 44-1418, space group P63/mcm).

nodes.characterization_summary: TEM, SAED, and XPS confirm pure Ni₃Sn₂ phase structure with nanoparticle morphology (Figures 1c, S2, S3).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM), selected area electron diffraction (SAED), and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) results further confirm the pure Ni₃Sn₂ phase structure with nanoparticle morphology (Figure 1c; Figures S2, and S3, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM image demonstrates ordered structure of Ni₃Sn₂ with interplanar spacing of 0.207 nm corresponding to (102) plane.
nodes.evidence_snippet: High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) image demonstrates the ordered structure of Ni₃Sn₂ with an interplanar spacing of 0.207 nm (Figure 1d), which corresponds to the (102) plane of Ni₃Sn₂.

nodes.characterization_summary: ICP-OES shows Sn gradually dissolves during activation of Ni₃Sn₂ with amount positively correlated with current density; only trace Sn dissolves, Ni dissolution negligible.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Inductively coupled plasma (ICP) results demonstrate that Sn gradually dissolves in the electrolyte. The dissolution amount is positively correlated with the current density (Figure 1f).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni 2p spectrum displays Ni³⁺ peak at 858.48 eV; Sn 3d peaks at 486.2 eV (Sn⁴⁺ 3d₅/₂) and 497.0 eV (Sn⁴⁺ 3d₃/₂) indicate oxidation of Sn to form SnO₃²⁻.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ni 2p spectrum displays a distinct Ni³⁺ peak at 858.48 eV, contrasting with the dominant Ni²⁺ peaks observed in the initial Ni₃Sn₂ (Figure 2a). Concurrently, the Sn 3d spectrum shows no peak corresponding to Sn⁰. The deconvoluted peaks at 486.2 and 497.0 eV are assigned to Sn⁴⁺ 3d₅/₂ and Sn⁴⁺ 3d₃/₂, respectively (Figure 2b).

nodes.characterization_summary: In situ Raman shows Ni-O bending at 473 cm⁻¹ and stretching at 557 cm⁻¹ for NiOOH; Sn-O vibration of SnO₃²⁻ at 577 cm⁻¹; δ/ν ratio of Ni₃Sn₂ (2.16-2.34) higher than Ni NPs (1.63-1.87) indicating larger interlayer spacing.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Two characteristic peaks appear at 473 and 557 cm⁻¹ when the applied potential exceeds 1.35 V, which correspond to δ (Ni-O) bending and ν (Ni-O) stretching vibrations of NiOOH. Additionally, the Sn-O vibration peak of SnO₃²⁻ at 577 cm⁻¹ further verifies the in situ formation of NiOOH-SnO₃²⁻ during electrochemical activation.

nodes.evidence_snippet: Consistent with this, thermogravimetric analysis (TGA) reveals a greater weight loss (2.05%) between 100-250°C for NiOOH-SnO₃²⁻ (Figure 2i).

nodes.evidence_snippet: In addition, FT-IR spectra reveal that NiOOH-SnO₃²⁻ exhibits stronger O-H stretching vibrations than NiOOH (Figure S7, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: EDS mapping confirms Ni and Sn elements uniformly distributed in Ni₃Sn₂ before and after activation (Figures 1h-k, S2).
nodes.evidence_snippet: Energy dispersive spectroscopy (EDS) mapping confirms that Ni and Sn elements are uniformly distributed (Figure S2, Supporting Information).

nodes.characterization_summary: HRTEM of activated Ni₃Sn₂ shows thin amorphous phase shell encapsulating crystalline core with lattice fringes less clear than before activation.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Compared with the clear lattice fringes before activation, the activated sample features a thin amorphous phase shell encapsulating the crystalline core (Figure 1g), implying surface structural reconstruction.
